title: YouTube: Is It a Reliable Source of Nutrition Information on COVID-19 Pandemic?
screen_reason: Cross-sectional analysis of Turkish-language YouTube videos on nutrition and COVID-19 (search from Turkey on 1 February 2021; first 280 results by relevance, 218 analysed after exclusions). Two nutrition-and-dietetics experts independently classified every video 'relevant' (scientifically correct) or 'misleading' (containing one or more scientifically unproven statements) against WHO, Turkish Dietetic Association and NICE guidance current at the video's publication date, with an external expert resolving discrepancies (ICC 0.90-1.00). The paper reports a verbatim share of items classified misleading (40/218 = 18.3 %), i.e. item-level falsity against an external ground truth with a stated denominator = CONTENT. The seven parallel instruments (JAMAS, mDISCERN, accuracy score, GQS, comprehensiveness, title-content consistency, audio-visual quality) are reported only as means and give no share.

estimates.country: Turkey (Turkish-language videos, search performed from Turkey)
estimates.measure_type: % of Turkish-language YouTube videos on nutrition and COVID-19 classified as misleading (containing one or more scientifically unproven statements)
estimates.value_raw: There were 178 (81.7%) fully relevant and 40 (18.3%) misleading videos [Table 1: n = 218; relevant n = 178; misleading n = 40]
estimates.denominator: 218 Turkish-language YouTube videos reviewed, from the first 280 results (sorted by the platform's default relevance ranking) after excluding non-Turkish videos, videos without audio/visual information, videos lacking coronavirus-and-nutrition content, duplicates and livestreams
estimates.definition: video classified 'misleading' because it contained one or more misleading, scientifically unproven statements when judged against guidelines from major public health agencies at the video's publication date; a video counted as misleading even if it also contained scientifically proven information
estimates.misinfo_def: Videos were classified as "relevant" if they contained scientifically correct information about nutrition during COVID 19 and as "misleading" if they contained scientifically unproven information. Videos were considered misleading if they contained one or more misleading scientifically unproven statements, as evaluated based on guidelines from major public health agencies (e.g., World Health Organization, Turkish Dietetic Association, and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence of England) at the video's publication date.
estimates.source_quote: The videos attracted a cumulative 6,258,694 views. There were 178 (81.7%) fully relevant and 40 (18.3%) misleading videos.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract; Results section 3 and Table 1 (Total videos n = 218; Relevant n = 178; Misleading n = 40); Discussion ('approximately 20% of the videos were misleading')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Preliminary review by nine intern dietitians; then all videos independently reviewed and analysed by two experts in nutrition and dietetics (E.I.-E., Z.B.) whose results were consolidated, with any discrepancy resolved by an external expert in nutrition and dietetics. Benchmarks: WHO food/nutrition COVID-19 guidance, Turkish Dietetic Association COVID-19 nutrition recommendations, and NICE's COVID-19 vitamin D evidence summary, as they stood at each video's publication date. Reliability reported: intraclass correlation coefficient for relevant/misleading classification, ICC range 0.90-1.00 ('excellent').
estimates.moderator_quote: The online video hosting resource YouTube was accessed on 1 February 2021 from Turkey using the search term "Coronavirus and nutrition" in Turkish language. ... The first 280 videos from search were included for further analysis. This screening strategy is based on previous studies indicating that the users do not go beyond the first few pages of results from a search engine. The results were sorted in decreasing order of relevance using the default YouTube algorithm.
estimates.notes: THRESHOLD / breadth note for an adjudicator: the misleading category is defined by 'scientifically unproven' statements, so a claim that is merely unsupported (not demonstrably false) counts, and a single such statement makes the whole video misleading even when the rest is accurate - the authors state this explicitly ('We considered a video misleading if it contained any misleading information in addition to scientifically proven information'). Hence breadth=misleading (loosest) rather than false. Rank-truncated frame (first 280 results by relevance) => denom_selection=curated; Turkish-language only, single time point, single platform (all stated limitations). Minor internal inconsistency: the abstract says the search term was 'nutrition and COVID-19' in Turkish while the Methods say 'Coronavirus and nutrition' in Turkish; and the Discussion counts the study's strength as 'the large number of videos (n = 280)' although 218 were analysed.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) NO VIEW-WEIGHTED (EXPOSURE) ROW IS DERIVABLE: the paper gives cumulative views (6,258,694) and mean views per video for relevant (24,975.3) and misleading (45,327.3) videos, but never a share of views going to misleading videos. Computing one would require multiplying means by counts (40 x 45,327.3 / 6,258,694), which is not a verbatim value nor an exact part/whole of verbatim counts, so R8 forbids it - even though the paper notes misleading videos were 'viewed more than twice more than the relevant videos' (not statistically significant, p = 0.582). (2) SOURCE SUBGROUPS NOT ROWED: Table 2 cross-tabulates misleading videos by uploader (news channels 4 of 25, health professionals 14 of 67, health centres 2 of 31, TV channels 9 of 27, government organisations 0 of 17, educational organisations 1 of 11, independent users 10 of 40); the text states 'Approximately 80% of the videos that shared by health professionals were relevant videos' and 'All of the videos that were uploaded by government organisations were relevant videos'. These are producer subgroups of the same corpus, not the paper's headline, so the whole-corpus figure was kept instead. NB the percentages in Table 2's Misleading column are shares OF THE 40 MISLEADING VIDEOS (e.g. health professionals 14 (35.0)), not within-source rates - an easy misreading for an adjudicator to check. (3) CONTENT SUBGROUPS: 'Approximately 20% of the boosting immune system videos and 25% of importance of physical activity videos were misleading' (156 and 8 videos respectively); topic subgroups of the same corpus, and the physical-activity cell has n = 8, so not extracted. (4) QUALITY INSTRUMENTS: JAMAS, mDISCERN, accuracy score, GQS, comprehensiveness score, title-content consistency index and audio-visual quality are all reported as means (SD) by group and by source, with no share above any threshold, so no QUALITY row is possible. (5) COMPARISON VALUES CITED FROM OTHER PAPERS (15-30 % of disease-related YouTube information misinforming; 2 of 72 videos in Khatri et al.; 27.5 % in Li et al.; 37.1 % in a Korean study) are excluded by R8. (6) Examples of the misleading nutrition claims are in Supplementary Table S9, which is not part of the text.

rob.design: Cross-sectional single-time-point YouTube content analysis. Frame: one Turkish-language keyword search ('Coronavirus and nutrition') run from Turkey on 1 February 2021 in a cleared-cache Chrome incognito session, results sorted by the default relevance algorithm; the first 280 videos were saved to a playlist (with URLs backed up) and 218 analysed after exclusions (non-Turkish, no audio/visual, off-topic, duplicates, livestreams). Coding: preliminary review by nine intern dietitians, then independent review of all videos by two nutrition-and-dietetics experts with consolidation and external-expert adjudication of discrepancies; relevant/misleading classification against WHO, Turkish Dietetic Association and NICE guidance at each video's publication date; seven additional scoring instruments applied. Reliability reported: ICC 0.90-1.00 for the relevant/misleading classification. Stated limitations: single time point on a dynamic platform, Turkish-language only, YouTube only. No external funding; no conflicts of interest declared; IRB not required (public data).
rob.item6_quote: Videos were considered misleading if they contained one or more misleading scientifically unproven statements, as evaluated based on guidelines from major public health agencies (e.g., World Health Organization [19–22], Turkish Dietetic Association [23,24], and National Institute for Health and Care Excellence of England [25]) at the video's publication date. We considered a video misleading if it contained any misleading information in addition to scientifically proven information because it still had the potential to disseminate misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: A total of 218 videos were reviewed and classified as "misleading" or "relevant" depending on the information provided. ... There were 178 (81.7%) fully relevant and 40 (18.3%) misleading videos.
